chapter: Grievances over Bolden, Bunk Johnson and Black bands
title: Elvis Presley comparison, and Tom Brown's death and the Times-Picayune article
summary: La Rocca says New Orleans media disgrace white men, describes the reporter's call after Tom Brown died, and introduces Averty's December 1956 letter.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Their champion was a colored man. Let's say a colored man has his rightful place in any music. Why not the white man to eulogize another man that hasn't created anything because of his color? That must be his music. But although Elvin Presley went on to hikes while the other guy stayed there, if you listen to his style, he couldn't have been original because he changed four or five different times. First his rhythm was based on the tango. Then he changed it to something else. Elvin Presley stuck to one style and he made a success. That's the difference when you come to New Orleans and you have pro-Negro people that runs papers, the press, radio, television, and so on. A white man does not have a chance. No matter what the white man has did, they try to disgrace him. I'll tell you the last thing that's been done to me, a dead man talking. When Tom Brown died, some man called me up on the phone and said, I'm from the Tynes, Picayune. My name is Mahima Allen. Is that you, Mr. LaRocca? He says, yeah. He says, you know, Tom Brown just died. I says, I'm very sorry to hear it. Yet I was suing this man. I was sorry to hear it because that wouldn't solve my problem by him dying. I wanted him. I wanted him to live. So I could bring him to court and implicate some of these chinges, what they call Eli people, but chinges to me. After he died, the Tynes, Picayune had an article in it. I'm going ahead of my story. He says, Tom Brown says he composed the Tiger Ragger. I says, Tom Brown's been an imposter all his life. I says, he composed nothing. I says, he never even composed the trombone parts he played, much less he copied them from Edwards. And I says, much less compose the music. And this guy says to me, can I use your name? I says, yes. I didn't know which way he was going to use it. Now, maybe they had a tape recorder. So in case I sued him, they could say, well, I give him the privilege to use the name. Because on a tape recorder, you can cut out, delete certain parts. Take the same tape and plant it into another machine and you got a full tape without anything being cut. I know those tricks and I've seen them did. I've never did them, but I've seen them done. And I know how it's done. So let me read this article that I had to Mr. Tom Brown that I had in the court at the time. I see the tape is getting low. Let me talk a little bit more on this thing. After he had passed away, the times pick a human hand in there, the Tom Brown who claims to have written the tiger rag, and Nick LaRocca who later copyrighted it under his name. Now, this man is dead, but he's talking after he's dead. Now, who put that in there, I don't know. But it can show you the type of people that you have on earth. Because I had this man just about to go into court when he died, probably. I hastened his death because he knew his jig was up and his lying days were over. I never knew that this was going on until I got a letter from a man in France one day telling me about what Tom Brown's claims were. His name is J.C. Avady of France. And this will give you an idea of how these people work. This is J.C. Avady, Paris, December 16, 1956. I'd like you to read this when this thing runs out because it's kind of a long letter. All right, we'll get it.
